title: Rows Times Squares
description: Stack rows of squares on a rectangle to see length x breadth, make a square for side x side, and split a length into three to find a breadth given as one third of it.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: See that rows times the squares in a row give the count, so the area of a rectangle is length x breadth and a square's is side x side, and find a breadth from a clue before multiplying.
writeup.look: A rectangle on squared paper with one row laid, the Rows handle up its breadth and the record card at the right; the Square switch on the third phase and the length strip with the Split button on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rows Times Squares' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of squares laid. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The rectangle lies on squared paper at x 120, y 250, drawn to one scale inside a box 620 by 400, its length along the bottom and labelled deep blue. The first row of violet squares, labelled Row, lies along the length. The Rows handle is a round grip at the rectangle's right edge that the child drags upward; each row it stacks lights amber for a moment. The record card stands at x 800, y 230, 300 by 260, with the columns Along the length, Along the breadth, Product and Count. The Units switch and the Square switch sit at x 800, y 520 and x 800, y 580. On the fourth phase the length strip lies at x 120, y 220, and the Split button at x 800, y 640 cuts it into three equal parts with two thin ink lines; one part drops down to stand as the breadth. The area reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with sq. cm and sq. m keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last rectangle stays filled with its rows, the record card beside it, and the area in green with its square unit.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the split part drops down beside the rectangle, the other two parts give a small nod, as if to say they are the same size.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet stacked. On the first phase a rectangle lies on squared paper with one row laid along its length and the Rows handle at its side. On the second a garden lies with its sides in metres and the Units switch set. On the third a board lies with the Square switch beside it. On the fourth a length strip lies above an empty rectangle, with a clue card and the Split button. One thing moves, once: the Rows handle, the Square switch or the Split button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any rectangle, stacked row by row, turned into a square, or given a breadth by the Split button. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rows times squares, length x breadth, side x side and a breadth from a clue.

observations.why: every row along the length holds the same number of squares.
observations.soWhat: rows times the squares in a row gives the count, the same as counting one by one.
observations.observe: Each row stacked added the same number of squares to the count.

observations.why: multiplying is a quicker way of adding equal rows.
observations.soWhat: the area of a rectangle is length x breadth.
observations.observe: The product on the record card always matched the count.

observations.why: a square's length and breadth are equal.
observations.soWhat: the area of a square is side x side.
observations.observe: When the Square switch pulled the breadth up, the two numbers in the product became the same.

observations.why: one third of a length is the length split into three equal parts.
observations.soWhat: find the breadth from the clue first, then multiply.
observations.observe: The split part stood beside the rectangle, much shorter than the length.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, no colour means good or bad. The miss empties the answer slot at once (every digit, every box, a picked choice), so it is empty through the traceback; the pad re-opens empty after it.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The rows light up again one at a time beside the count, and the line ends on length x breadth = the count.
Phase 2: The rows of unit squares light up again, then the line ends on length x breadth = the area with its square unit.
Phase 3: The rows of the square light up again, then the line ends on side x side = the area in sq. cm.
Phase 4: The split part stands as the breadth and the rows light up again, then the line ends on length x breadth = the area.

voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: A rectangle on squared paper has 9 squares along its length and 5 along its breadth. How many squares does it cover?

question.en: Stack the rows, then say how many squares cover this 9 by 5 rectangle.

items.planQuestion: A rectangle on squared paper has 6 squares along its length and 4 along its breadth. How many squares does it cover?

question.en: Now stack the rows of a 6 by 4 rectangle and find how many squares it covers.

items.planQuestion: A rectangle on squared paper has 12 squares along its length and 8 along its breadth. How many squares does it cover?

question.en: How many squares cover a rectangle 12 squares long and 8 squares wide?

items.planQuestion: A garden is 16 m long and 7 m wide. What is its area?

question.en: Fill this 16 m by 7 m garden and find its area in square metres.

items.planQuestion: A card is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide. What is its area?

question.en: A card is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide, so what is its area in square centimetres?

items.planAnswer: 8 x 6 = 48, so the area of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle is 48 sq. cm

items.planQuestion: A floor is 14 m long and 9 m wide. What is its area?

question.en: Find the area in square metres of a floor 14 m long and 9 m wide.

items.planAnswer: 14 x 9 = 126, so the area of a 14 m by 9 m rectangle is 126 sq. m

items.planQuestion: A square board has sides of 15 cm. What is its area?

question.en: Turn the board into a 15 cm square; what is its area in square centimetres?

items.planQuestion: A square stamp has sides of 4 cm. What is its area?

question.en: This stamp is a square of side 4 cm; what is its area in square centimetres?

items.planAnswer: 4 x 4 = 16, so the area of a square of side 4 cm is 16 sq. cm

items.planQuestion: A square tile has sides of 20 cm. What is its area?

question.en: What is the area in square centimetres of a square tile with sides of 20 cm?

items.planQuestion: A rectangle is 27 cm long, and its breadth is one third of its length. What is its area?

question.en: Its length is 27 cm and its breadth one third of that; find the area.
Now the length is 24 cm and the breadth is a third of it; what is the area?

items.planQuestion: A rectangle is 33 m long, and its breadth is one third of its length. What is its area?

question.en: A rectangle is 33 m long and one third of that wide; what is its area?

items.planAnswer: One third of 33 m is 11 m, because 3 x 11 = 33. The area of a 33 m by 11 m rectangle is 33 x 11 = 363 sq. m
